segments.text: Before we get started, I want to give a huge shout out to Squarespace for sponsoring this video.
So guys, in this video, I'm going to be laying out my four best strategies for preventing muscle loss
in a caloric deficit based on the scientific literature. But before we get into those,
I think it's important that we first understand why it is that we're more likely to lose muscle
on a diet in the first place. Now, so in any scenario, whether you gain or lose muscle is going to be
dictated by the balance between muscle protein synthesis and muscle protein breakdown. If you
synthesize more muscle than you break down, you gain net muscle, and if you break down more
muscle than you synthesize, you're going to lose net muscle. And you can think of this as if
your muscle were a brick wall and whether the wall gets higher is going to be determined by
whether you're adding more bricks or removing more bricks over time. The individual bricks are
muscle proteins. So with this in mind, let's quickly cover the four main causes of muscle loss
on a diet. First, you have suppressed rates of muscle protein synthesis. You're not adding bricks
to the wall as quickly anymore. Second, you have greater rates of muscle protein breakdown. So now
you're actively removing bricks from the wall more quickly. And third, you're using more protein
as fuel. So the more protein you burn off as energy, the less protein that will be available
to help build the wall. And then finally, you may just lose strength in the gym as you get leaner.
Remember from my video on bare mode that all else equal a bigger body is going to be a stronger body.
So if you're progressively handling heavier weights over time, it's going to cause more tension on
the muscle and a greater signal for growth as well. And by the same token, if you're handling
progressively lighter weights over time as you get weaker and leaner, there's going to be less
tension on the muscle, less of a signal for growth and less muscle retention as a result.
And of course, this doesn't mean that you should always lift as heavy as possible since we also
know that training volume really matters as well. And if you're always lifting with maximum load,
then you may not be able to do as many sets. But still, I would say that losing strength is a
potential cause of muscle loss. And you can sort of think of strength training as the lead
construction boss, if he's no longer there, giving out orders and the walls probably not going to
get built. Okay, so with the four causes of muscle loss in mind, now let's lay out the four best
science-based strategies for minimizing muscle loss on a cut. So first, you really do want to do
your best to maintain your strength levels in the gym. I find many people have the temptation to
start training with higher reps to sweat more and burn more calories during training. However,
this may actually be contributing to muscle loss because you're no longer placing the same
tensile stimulus on the muscle. And also just because you're sweating more or it feels like
you're working harder, that doesn't necessarily mean that you're actually burning more calories.
And in my opinion, I think you'd be much better off using diet and cardio to establish the
caloric deficit rather than just bumping up the reps. And so I think the real question is how
should we structure our training when dieting? In other words, how do training requirements change
when you go from a caloric surplus to a caloric deficit? And I think the answer is actually quite
simple. It doesn't. In the words of Dr. Eric Helms, your training requirements don't change
only your ability to recover changes. And so I think you should make your goal to maintain your
strength in the gym for as long as you can. Meaning at the start of your cut, you shouldn't
lighten loads right away, start switching up your exercises or reduce volume. I think the
bread and butter heavy compound lifts should stay in your program and you should make it your
goal to maintain your strength on those, working mostly in the 6 to 12 reps zone. Let's put
another way. You should try to maintain the weight you can do for 6 to 12 reps on as many movements
as possible for as long as possible. And in my opinion, this is going to be the single best way
to maintain your muscle mass on a cut. Of course, there will come a point where you're going to
start feeling more banged up from your training and what used to feel really light or really easy,
suddenly going to start to feel really heavy. And that basically just means that your ability to
recover is decreasing. And at that point, I think you should reduce your training volume by removing
a few sets before reducing the weight that you're using. And at a certain point, you may need to
reduce both the volume and the load so that you don't over train or get injured. But that usually
shouldn't come until after months of dieting and it'll get more pronounced as you get, say below
the 8 to 10% body fat zone for men and 15 to 18% for women. I'm so at the first few months of your
diet. I think you really should make your best efforts to maintain your strength levels in the gym
for as long as you can. Okay, so my second strategy is going to be to diet more slowly. I'm to
understand this. Let's take a look at a 2011 study from Garth and colleagues which took 30 elite
athletes with 10 to 13 years of training experience on average and put them either in a slow reduction
group where they slashed 469 calories per day for nine weeks or a fast reduction group
where they slashed 791 calories for five weeks. Both groups lost the same amount of weight,
and while fast fat loss may sound more appealing at first, when you look at the full results here,
you can see that the slow diet group actually had much more favorable outcomes where the slow
group lost 4.9 kilograms of fat and actually gained 1 kilogram of muscle, whereas the fast group
only lost 3.2 kilograms of fat and also lost 0.2 kilograms of muscle. So based on this research,
it seems that a slower rate of weight loss is probably better at preserving muscle. However,
I don't think that's to say that you should diet as slowly as possible and just take an
eternity to actually get lean. And earlier paper from Dr. Gilbert Forbes found that there are in fact
two factors at play here, the size of the deficit, but also the starting body fat of the person,
meaning that at the beginning of a diet when you have more body fat to lose, I think you can be
a bit more aggressive with the caloric deficit and then as you get leaner, you should start to lose
more slowly. On a landmark 2014 paper, Dr. Eric Helms and colleagues recommended 0.5 to 1% of
body weight loss per week for maximum muscle retention. And personally I found that at the start of
a diet, you can raise this figure as high as 1.5%, especially if you have a nice bit of weight to lose,
and then the target gets smaller the leaner you get. So let's say you're doing a 12-week diet,
you can aim to lose 1 to 1.5% of body weight per week for the first few weeks, around 1% for the
middle chunk, and then 0.5% for the final few weeks. So assuming a 200 pound individual,
that'd be three pounds per week for the first chunk, two pounds per week for the middle,
and then one pound per week toward the end. So when you add all that up, it's 24 pounds lost with
most of it being fat and water, not muscle. Okay, so strategy number three is to increase your protein
intake. In 2018, researchers out of Dr. Stu Phillips lab found that 2.4 grams of protein per
kilogram, so about 1 gram per pound of body weight, was able to preserve lean body mass on a 40%
energy deficit when combined with resistance exercise. Now some data out of Dr. Jose Antonio's lab
has suggested potential benefits. I'm going as high as 4.4 grams per kilogram. They're just about
2 grams per pound. However, this data hasn't yet been replicated in most studies, seemed to land
somewhere between 0.8 to 1 gram per pound of body weight as a pretty solid upper limit
past which you don't really see better outcomes for muscle masking or retention. And finally,
my last tip is to avoid excessive cardio from 2014. Helms and colleagues concluded that natural
bodybuilders should perform the lowest number in duration of cardio sessions possible, while still
meeting their need to reduce body fat in order to avoid interference with strength training.
As a coach personally, I generally recommend no more than 1-2 HIT sessions per week, maybe 4-5
low intensity steady state sessions and only as needed to establish the caloric deficit when
diet alone isn't enough. And I think maybe I'll cover the interference effect in a little more detail
in a future video if you guys would like to see that. So guys, those are my top 4 strategies for
preserving muscle mass on a cut. Now you guys can let me know in the comments below if there's
